prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Your, And, Our

outputs.L1:
Your first dog is forever your one dog,  
and no story has a happy ending anymore.  
We have all wasted lives; sometimes, we waste  
our own. Some nights are long; some  
never end at all. I don’t know how we can  
fall in love, which implies landing,  
whereas love promises everything but.  

That’s why I like to listen to birds calling  
to each other at dusk from the acacias.  
But then I remember it is still daylight, and I  
hear them in the absence of the trees.  

When I travel by train over mountains,  
all I think of is the sea. My father was  
never quite so alive until he died, and now  
he is immortal. Somebody must do the calculus;  
somebody must work out the logic of the logic  
of this spectacle—because “spectacle” is the last  
word anyone would use for dreams that do not cease,  
for the sound of weeping from the next room.  
Only there is no next room, and we are the only ones  
there, though only for a moment—and a lifetime more.  

Listen: I will tell you a secret, the secret you once told  
me on the train into the mountains,  
on the journey to the shore, long ago, when  
we spoke and never met. That secret, which is ours.  

Some nights are so long that the old dog comes home  
to those of us who remain there, waiting and waiting,  
even if we have never been here before, where we are.
outputs.L2:
The first dog you love remains the only dog, and stories no longer conclude with happiness. Every life has been squandered; at times, the life we throw away is our own. Certain nights stretch on, while others never finish.

I cannot understand why entering love is called falling, as though an arrival were involved, when love guarantees anything except solid ground. Perhaps this is why, at twilight, I enjoy hearing birds answer one another among the acacias. Then I remember that the sun is still up and that the calls reach me where no trees exist.

Whenever a train carries me across the mountains, the ocean occupies my thoughts. My father achieved his greatest vitality only after his death; now he cannot die. Someone must calculate it all, must determine the reasoning behind reason in this display—though “display” is the last name anyone would give to unending dreams or to sobbing heard beyond the wall, when there is no adjoining room and no one is present except us, briefly and for another lifetime.

Listen: I’m going to share a confidence—the same one you once gave me aboard the mountain-bound train as we traveled toward the coast. It happened long ago, when we talked without ever meeting. The secret belongs to both of us.

On nights that endure long enough, the old dog returns to those of us who are still here, waiting without end, even though we have never previously stood in this place we now inhabit.
outputs.L3:
The first dog retains a unique emotional significance, representing an attachment that cannot be replaced or fully overcome. Its memory brings together love and loss, suggesting that some bonds remain permanent precisely because they have ended. In this sense, the dog also symbolizes the impossibility of completely happy endings: affection may endure, but it cannot prevent separation, death, or longing.

Love itself is portrayed as paradoxical and disorienting. It seems to promise permanence, intimacy, and a final sense of belonging, yet it never allows the speaker to feel that they have securely arrived. Instead, love creates uncertainty, making presence inseparable from the fear or memory of absence. The natural world reinforces this instability. Birds, trees, mountains, and the sea do not simply represent what is visible; they become reminders of what is missing. Memory transforms the landscape, blurring the boundary between external reality and inner grief.

This process is especially powerful in relation to the father’s death. Although he is physically absent, memory makes him feel more vivid, present, and even immortal. Death does not erase him but changes the form of his existence: he survives in recollections, dreams, habits, and shared secrets. As grief reshapes experience, ordinary distinctions between past and present, near and far, reality and imagination begin to collapse. The dead seem capable of returning, while the living remain caught in a state of expectation. They wait for reunions they know are impossible, sustained by memories that preserve love even as they continually renew the pain of loss.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores grief, love, memory, and mortality through a sequence of paradoxical reflections and dreamlike images. Rather than presenting loss as a single event that can be understood and overcome, it portrays grief as an unstable condition in which absence becomes a powerful form of presence. The dead are gone, yet they remain intimately connected to the speaker’s inner life; the past has ended, yet it continues to shape every act of remembering and longing. In this way, the poem resists the ordinary boundaries between life and death, presence and absence, departure and return.

Its images of dogs, birds, trains, mountains, and the sea create a world that is both familiar and strange. Animals appear as instinctive witnesses or guides, seemingly able to cross boundaries that human beings cannot. Birds suggest freedom, distance, and the possibility of communication between different realms, while dogs evoke loyalty, companionship, and the persistence of love beyond separation. Trains introduce movement and irreversible time: they carry people away, connect distant places, and imply journeys whose destinations may remain unknown. The mountains and the sea enlarge the poem’s emotional landscape, placing private sorrow against forces that seem timeless and immeasurable. These natural and symbolic elements do not resolve grief, but they give it a shape.

At the center of the poem is the absent father. His absence is not portrayed as emptiness alone. Instead, he survives through memory, imagination, and the speaker’s continued desire for connection. The father may be unreachable in a literal sense, but he remains present in the speaker’s perception of the world. Ordinary sights become reminders of him, while dreams and memories allow past and present to overlap. The speaker’s love therefore preserves what death has taken away, even as that preservation makes the pain of loss more enduring.

The poem’s paradoxes express this complicated emotional truth. To lose someone is, in one sense, to discover how permanently that person has entered one’s life. Separation intensifies attachment; distance creates a new kind of closeness; death fixes the beloved in memory. The speaker appears to move forward through time while also being repeatedly drawn backward, returning to scenes, feelings, and possibilities that can no longer be recovered. Memory is both consolation and wound: it keeps love alive, but it also continually reveals what is missing.

This tension shapes the poem’s idea of home. Home is not simply a physical place or a secure point in the past. It is imagined as something the speaker longs to return to, even though it may never have existed in a complete or accessible form. The desired home might be childhood, reunion with the father, freedom from mortality, or a state in which love is untouched by loss. Because such a home cannot be fully remembered or reached, it becomes a place of expectation as much as recollection—a home that seems to wait in the future while calling from the past.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that longing transforms our experience of time. The dead remain with us because love refuses to confine them to what is over. Memory allows the past to enter the present, while hope imagines reunion beyond the limits of ordinary life. Through its shifting, dreamlike imagery, the poem presents grief not as a journey toward forgetting but as an ongoing relationship with absence. Loss makes the beloved unreachable, yet also enduringly present, returning the speaker again and again to a mysterious home never fully known but continually remembered, desired, and awaited.
outputs.L5:
### Your, And, Our

**Your** ideas bring a perspective no one else can offer.  
**And** when they meet the thoughts, experiences, and hopes of others, something new becomes possible.  
**Our** shared effort turns individual dreams into collective progress.

Your voice matters. And together, our voices can create understanding, inspire change, and build a future that belongs to everyone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about grief, memory, love, a deceased father, and the lasting bond with one’s first dog, using surreal contradictions and dreamlike imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
My father keeps dying in the next room,  
though the next room was demolished years ago.

At night, I hear him folding the dark  
into neat squares,  
placing each one in a drawer  
where his shirts still remember his shoulders.

Grief is a window made of stone.  
I open it  
and the whole house enters me—

the clock drinking backward,  
the hallway kneeling in its own dust,  
his laughter asleep beneath the table  
with its shoes still on.

And there is my first dog,  
young again in the country of no calendars,  
running through fields of blue snow,  
carrying the sun gently in his mouth.

He does not know he is dead.  
Or I do not know I am living.  
Between us, the years wag their invisible tail.

My father whistles.  
The dog lifts his head.  
Somewhere, a door closes  
and becomes a road.

I follow until morning,  
when the dream breaks without shattering,  
when love—impossible animal—  
curls at the foot of my bed.

I reach down.

My hand passes through fur,  
through ash,  
through the warm, unanswering air—

and still,  
something leans into my palm.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a melancholic prose poem in the style of contemporary literary poetry, featuring birds at dusk, a train crossing mountains toward the sea, an old dog returning home, and a secret shared between two people who never met.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk, the birds loosen from the telephone wires, one by one, like words a mouth has grown too tired to keep. Their wings darken the last blue above the fields. Far off, a train enters the mountains, carrying its lit windows toward the sea. From the valley, it looks almost tender—a small, bright sentence passing through stone.

The old dog returns by the road he left years ago. Burrs in his coat, rain in his bones, he pauses at each gate as if waiting for the world to remember him. At the final house, no one calls his name. Still, he lies down on the porch, placing his gray muzzle between his paws, faithful to a door that has forgotten how to open.

Once, two people who never met kept the same secret. Each believed it belonged to them alone: that grief is not the absence of love, but its final country. One wrote it in a letter and burned it. The other whispered it into a sleeping room. Between them stretched cities, winters, the long machinery of chance.

Now the train descends toward salt air. The birds vanish into the dusk. Somewhere, the dog dreams the house as it was—warm hands, a bowl filled, his name rising through summer.

The sea waits beyond the mountains, practicing its endless arrival.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an elegiac poem that begins with “Your first dog is ever your one dog” and explores how death makes people immortal, how love defies logic, and how longing distorts time and place.
counterfactuals.output:
Your first dog is ever your one dog,  
though others sleep later beside the fire,  
twitching through fields you cannot enter.  
The heart keeps no sensible ledger.  
It spends what is gone, calls loss desire.  

Death makes its poor amendments:  
the body, once ordinary as rain,  
becomes untouchable, everywhere—  
a name no years can weather,  
a face time cannot persuade to age.  

So the dead inherit immortality  
not in heaven, but in us:  
in the cup we still set down softly,  
the stair whose third board speaks,  
the door we glance toward at dusk.  

Love has never understood proof.  
It chooses the vanished over the visible,  
one voice over the choir of the living,  
one hand’s remembered weight  
against the evidence of empty air.  

And longing deranges the compass.  
A room becomes a country;  
a winter afternoon lasts thirty years.  
The old yard waits behind every gate,  
the lost house stands inside each house.  

Sometimes, crossing a street at twilight,  
you are suddenly where you were—  
young, called home, forgiven—  
while beside you runs that faithful shape,  
still warm, still breathless, never gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-stanza, stream-of-consciousness poem about loss and impossible homecomings. Include paradoxes, enjambment, philosophical reflections, and recurring images of long nights, absent rooms, mountains, and the shore.
counterfactuals.output:
The long night enters the absent room before I do,  
though I have never left, though leaving is the only road  
that knows my name, and beyond the window the mountains  
kneel upward, stone prayers refusing every heaven; I think  
loss is what remains when nothing stays, a door still opening  
after the house is gone, and I cross its threshold into another  
long night where your chair is an absent room, your voice  
a silence speaking clearly from the shore—always the shore,  
with its patient argument of arrival and erasure, the waves  
coming home by breaking, going nowhere by return. Perhaps  
to be is only to misremember nonbeing, perhaps love  
is the wound that heals by deepening, and I carry you  
like an empty cup overflowing, climb the mountains by descending  
into their shadow, call this exile home because home is impossible  
and therefore everywhere: in the absent rooms behind my eyes,  
in the long nights that end without ending, in each grain of shore  
the sea takes back and gives away, while I walk toward you  
with every step leading farther, while the mountains grow smaller  
and heavier inside me, while the house lights its vanished lamps,  
while you stand in no room at all and ask why I am late,  
and I answer I arrived before I was born, I will return  
after returning is lost, I am here, I am almost here, listen—  
the long night is knocking from within the absent room,  
the mountains are dreaming they are waves, and the shore  
keeps drawing our names where nothing can keep them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a haunting surrealist poem in which the speaker mourns a father and a dog, hears birds in trees that are not there, remembers a mysterious train journey, and ends with the sense of waiting somewhere they have never been before.
counterfactuals.output:
My father left his coat on the moon,  
its pockets full of extinguished matches.  
The dog followed, nose to the ash,  
dragging his chain through my sleep.

Now every room smells faintly of rain  
and the dark fur behind his ears.  
I call them both at dusk,  
but only the staircase turns its head.

Outside, birds clamor in trees  
that are not there—  
black throats opening among invisible branches,  
wings beating holes in the air.

Once, we boarded a train without windows.  
Father held a ticket printed in salt.  
The dog lay beneath the seat, dreaming  
of a field that moved beside us.

No conductor came. No stations passed.  
Still, someone whispered our names  
from the next carriage, slowly,  
as if learning how to mourn.

I woke with soot beneath my tongue  
and a leash tied around my wrist.  
Far off, the absent trees were singing.  
The rails shone through the floor.

Now I sit beneath a clock with no hands,  
beside luggage I do not remember packing,  
waiting for them to return—  
waiting in a place I have never been before.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
